sourceHtml:
Felix Rieseberg, an engineering manager at Anthropic, has scrapped the classic coding interview. He argues that AI makes the tests pointless and that ambitious young developers can use it to overtake more experienced colleagues.

Rieseberg, who has led development of Claude.ai and Claude Code Desktop at Anthropic, says there's no longer any reason to give candidates small programming tasks. Claude now handles them better than the candidates do, he says. In his view, handing someone a little React challenge makes as little sense today as quizzing them on Assembly.

On his teams, good test scores no longer predict who turns out to be a top developer. Instead, he's watching relatively new engineers overtake more experienced colleagues. "Hunger beats tenure," he says. Rieseberg aims his post at "junior" developers, though he deliberately redefines the term. He doesn't necessarily mean people just starting out. He means any engineer without social status, power, or a network inside their company.

Why newcomers spot the problems veterans stopped seeing

Rieseberg argues that newcomers have a structural advantage because they notice problems that long-time employees accepted as givens years ago. He points to organizational researcher James March, who wrote in 1991 that organizations depend on a steady stream of naive and uninformed newcomers. Stripe founder Patrick Collison has also explicitly urged new hires to flag anything that seems strange to them. Veterans, he noted, stopped noticing those friction points long ago.

Rieseberg cites his time at Notion as an example. He was asked to design an offline architecture that people inside the company considered impossible. The data model was too complex, and CEO Ivan Zhao would supposedly never accept the only workable solution. The technical hurdle was real, but the founder's resistance wasn't. Nobody had asked him, because everyone treated it as common knowledge.

Cheap execution weakens the old hierarchy

The core problem for newcomers, Rieseberg says, is that nobody in the company listens to them. Because execution used to be expensive, organizations were built so that a few decision-makers could approve or block ideas. You had to work your way up a rigid hierarchy before management trusted you to actually build something. AI changes that equation because execution is no longer expensive, Rieseberg writes.

His first piece of advice builds on a 2011 quote from Patrick McKenzie, who wrote that "engineers are hired to create business value, not to program things." Developers should understand what their company is really trying to achieve and attach themselves to the parts that make money. A useful starting point is knowing your manager's manager's goals.

From there, he suggests picking an ambitious idea that would dramatically advance those goals and building a working prototype over a weekend. That skips the usual cycle of product specs, approvals, and lobbying designers or product managers. The key is to focus on one good idea instead of hiding three good ones among 20 bad ones. Anyone who builds a prototype that includes a new programming language, a backend, and mobile apps all at once will fail. The prototype should get the idea across so clearly that leadership immediately sees both the opportunity and the right person to run with it.

Newcomers have the edge on empathy

Rieseberg distinguishes between two types of engineers. Newcomers working on user-facing products bring a natural empathy for outside users. Long-tenured colleagues at Slack or Notion had a hard time seeing things from an outside user's perspective. Engineers working on infrastructure or internal tools, on the other hand, benefit from not knowing why something is supposed to be impossible.

He backs this up with an example from his own company. Two Anthropic engineers who were relatively new at the time, Anthony Morris and Alice Zhao, built the graphical interface for Claude Code over a weekend. The first public version shipped about eight days later.

Rieseberg now looks for small prototypes in job applications that show taste, empathy, and principled thinking. The classic coding interview isn't coming back, he says.

On one hand, Rieseberg's advice reads as a message of empowerment. AI becomes an equalizer that lets newcomers get past gatekeepers who've gone blind to their own company's problems. On the other hand, it moves the bar for entry-level jobs away from diligence and craft toward entrepreneurial thinking, product sense, and taste. Most universities barely teach those skills, and companies have traditionally expected them from experienced product managers or founders.

The engineers he holds up as models also build prototypes on weekends without being asked. "Hunger beats tenure" sounds motivating, but it assumes a hustle mentality that not every new developer can bring to the job.

translation.html:
Anthropic 工程经理 Felix Rieseberg 已经取消了传统的编程面试。他认为，AI 让这类测试失去了意义，而有抱负的年轻开发者可以借助 AI 超越经验更丰富的同事。

Rieseberg 曾在 Anthropic 主导 Claude.ai 和 Claude Code Desktop 的开发。他表示，已经没有理由再给候选人布置小型编程任务了，因为如今 Claude 完成这些任务的表现比候选人更好。在他看来，今天让人做一道小型 React 挑战题，就像考他们 Assembly（汇编语言）一样没什么意义。

在他的团队里，测试成绩好已经无法预测谁最终会成为顶尖开发者。相反，他正看到资历较浅的工程师超越经验更丰富的同事。“渴望胜过资历，”他说。Rieseberg 这篇帖子面向的是“初级”开发者，不过他有意重新定义了这个词。他指的不一定是刚入行的人，而是在公司内部没有地位、权力或人脉的任何工程师。

为什么新人能发现老员工早已视而不见的问题

Rieseberg 认为，新人具有结构性优势，因为他们会注意到一些问题，而老员工多年前就已将这些问题视为理所当然。他提到，组织研究学者 James March 在 1991 年曾写道，组织依赖源源不断、天真且不了解情况的新人。Stripe 创始人 Patrick Collison 也曾明确鼓励新员工指出任何让他们觉得奇怪的事情。他指出，老员工早就注意不到这些阻碍了。

Rieseberg 以自己在 Notion 的经历为例。当时，他受命设计一种离线架构，而公司内部的人认为这不可能实现。数据模型过于复杂，而且据说首席执行官 Ivan Zhao 绝不会接受唯一可行的解决方案。技术障碍确实存在，但创始人的反对却并不存在。没有人问过他，因为大家都把这当成了常识。

低成本的执行削弱了旧有层级

Rieseberg 说，新人面临的核心问题是，公司里没有人听他们的意见。由于过去执行成本高昂，组织的架构使少数决策者能够批准或否决想法。在管理层信任你、让你真正动手做出东西之前，你必须沿着严格的层级一步步往上爬。Rieseberg 写道，AI 改变了这种局面，因为执行已经不再昂贵。

他的第一条建议基于 Patrick McKenzie 在 2011 年的一句话：“雇用工程师是为了创造商业价值，而不是编写程序。”开发者应当理解公司真正想要实现什么，并让自己参与到能赚钱的业务中。一个实用的起点，是了解你上司的上司的目标。

在此基础上，他建议选一个能大幅推动这些目标实现的大胆想法，用一个周末做出可运行的原型。这样就能跳过通常的产品规格说明、审批，以及游说设计师或产品经理的流程。关键是专注于一个好想法，而不是把三个好想法藏在 20 个坏想法中。任何人如果试图在一个原型中同时囊括一门新编程语言、一个后端和多个移动应用，都会失败。原型应当把想法表达得足够清楚，让领导层立即看出其中的机会，以及谁是推进这件事的合适人选。

新人在同理心方面更有优势

Rieseberg 区分了两类工程师。从事面向用户产品开发的新人，天然更能理解外部用户的感受。在 Slack 或 Notion 工作多年的同事，很难从外部用户的角度看问题。而从事基础设施或内部工具开发的工程师，则会因为不知道某件事为什么被认为不可能实现而受益。

他用自己公司的一个例子来佐证这一点。当时加入 Anthropic 不久的两名工程师 Anthony Morris 和 Alice Zhao，用一个周末做出了 Claude Code 的图形界面。大约八天后，第一个公开版本就发布了。

Rieseberg 现在会在求职申请中寻找能够体现品位、同理心和原则性思考的小型原型。他表示，传统的编程面试不会回来了。

一方面，Rieseberg 的建议读起来像是在为新人赋能。AI 成为一种拉平差距的工具，让新人能够绕过那些已对自家公司问题视而不见的把关者。另一方面，这也把初级岗位的门槛从勤勉和技术功底，转向了创业思维、产品意识和品位。大多数大学几乎不教这些能力，而公司传统上会要求经验丰富的产品经理或创始人具备这些能力。

他树为榜样的工程师，也会在无人要求的情况下利用周末制作原型。“渴望胜过资历”听起来鼓舞人心，但它预设了一种拼搏心态，而并非每位新开发者都能以这种心态投入工作。
